sources.name: Conservation Assessment for the Northern Goshawk in Southeast Alaska
sources.publisher: USDA Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Research Station
source_locators: The assessment defines Tongass old-growth sawtimber as over 150 years old while noting that the full complement of old-growth features may not occur until about 250 years.
It reports 405,000 acres of productive old growth harvested from 1954–1995 and estimates another 45,000 acres from 1909–1954, for 450,000 acres total.
The assessment reports about 5.6 million acres of productive forest and states that clearcut even-aged management was the predominant harvest method.

sources.name: Tongass National Forest: Forest Service’s Actions Related to Its Planned Timber Program Transition
source_locators: GAO states that the Tongass timber program had been based on harvesting old-growth trees since the early twentieth century and that the transition to young growth was announced in 2010.
Forest Service data reviewed by GAO show average annual timber-related expenditures of $12.5 million and revenues of $1.1 million from fiscal years 2005–2014.
The expenditure figure excludes road construction and maintenance; the receipt therefore does not add an estimated road cost.

metric_contract.unit: productive old-growth acres harvested, explicit age definition, accumulated duration, forest share and realized timber-program fiscal burden
metric_contract.geography: Tongass National Forest, southeast Alaska, United States
metric_contract.assessment_period: cumulative old-growth harvest from 1909–1995 and federal timber-program expenditures and revenues from fiscal years 2005–2014
metric_contract.boundary: The Forest Service old-growth and productive-forest definitions are retained. The receipt does not label all mature forest as old growth, add conveyed non-federal lands, infer carbon emissions, or include unreported road costs.

uncertainty: The 45,000-acre 1909–1954 quantity is estimated from reported saw-log volume and an assumed per-acre harvest volume, while the 405,000-acre 1954–1995 quantity is inventory-based. Productive forest is a timber-capability class and is not identical to the old-growth denominator in every ecological interpretation. The 2005–2014 fiscal figures cover the Tongass timber program during a period when GAO describes the program as historically old-growth-based, but the figures are not allocated sale-by-sale between old and young growth. Net public cost excludes road construction and maintenance and is an administrative fiscal burden, not an ecological valuation.
